title: Erdős Problem #221: Additive Complements with Powers of 2
description: Is there a set A ⊆ ℕ with |A ∩ {1,...,N}| ≪ N/log N such that every large integer can be written as 2^k + a for some k ≥ 0 and a ∈ A? SOLVED: YES, by Ruzsa (1972) using an ingenious construction based on powers of 5.

meta.author: Lorentz (1954), Ruzsa (1972, 2001)
originalContributions: density_lower_bound axiom: optimality of N/log N
primitive_root_order axiom: multiplicative order of 2 mod 5^n
powers_cover_residues axiom: coverage of coprime residues

overview.historicalContext:
Erdős Problem #221 belongs to the intersection of additive combinatorics and multiplicative number theory. The question arose naturally from the study of additive complements: given a set B, how sparse can a set A be while still ensuring A + B covers all large integers?

The powers of 2 are a canonical example of a lacunary (exponentially sparse) sequence — there are only about log₂ N of them up to N. Erdős asked whether their additive complement could have density as low as O(N/log N), the natural threshold suggested by the sparsity of the powers.

George G. Lorentz (1954) gave the first positive answer in his paper 'On a problem of additive number theory', constructing a complement with the slightly weaker density O(N log log N / log N). The extra log log N factor seemed difficult to remove.

Imre Z. Ruzsa (1972) achieved the breakthrough, eliminating the log log N factor entirely with an elegant construction based on an unexpected connection to primitive roots. His key observation: 2 is a primitive root modulo 5^n for all n ≥ 1 (a classical fact from algebraic number theory). This means powers of 2 cover all residues coprime to 5^n, which can be leveraged to build sparse complements. The construction A = {5^n · m : 5^n ≥ C log m} + {0,1} with C = 1/(5 log 2) achieves density O(N/log N).

In 2001, Ruzsa refined the construction in 'Additive completion of lacunary sequences' to achieve the asymptotically exact density N/log₂ N. A matching lower bound shows this is optimal up to the leading constant.
overview.problemStatement: Is there a set A ⊆ ℕ such that: (1) |A ∩ {1,...,N}| ≪ N/log N for all large N, and (2) every large integer can be written as 2^k + a for some k ≥ 0 and a ∈ A?
overview.proofStrategy: Ruzsa's construction: A = { 5^n · m : m ≥ 1 and 5^n ≥ C log m } + {0, 1} where C = 1/(5 log 2). The key insight is that 2 is a primitive root modulo 5^n for all n ≥ 1, meaning powers of 2 cover all residues coprime to 5^n. This ensures every large integer has the required representation while the constraint 5^n ≥ C log m keeps A sparse.
keyInsights: The fundamental tension in additive complement problems: powers of 2 are exponentially sparse ($\sim \log_2 N$ elements up to $N$), yet their complement $A$ needs only $O(N/\log N)$ elements — vastly more than the powers themselves but still vanishing as a fraction of $[N]$.

Ruzsa's key insight is the connection to primitive roots: 2 is a primitive root mod $5^n$ for all $n \ge 1$, meaning $\{2^0, 2^1, \ldots\}$ mod $5^n$ covers all coprime residues. This algebraic structure converts a number-theoretic property into additive coverage.

The choice of 5 is not arbitrary but optimal: it is the smallest odd prime $p$ for which 2 is a primitive root mod $p^n$ for all $n$. The 'lifting' from $p$ to all $p^n$ is a special property (Hensel's lemma alone does not guarantee it for primitive roots).

The density $N/\log N$ is tight from both sides: Ruzsa's construction achieves $O(N/\log N)$ as an upper bound, while a pigeonhole argument shows any complement needs $\Omega(N/\log N)$ elements. This completely determines the order of magnitude.

The $\{0,1\}$ padding in Ruzsa's set handles parity: since all powers of 2 except $2^0 = 1$ are even, an odd integer $n$ cannot be written as $2^k + a$ with $k \ge 1$ unless $a$ is odd. Adding both parities to the core set resolves this.

sections.title: Basic Definitions
sections.summary: Defines PowersOfTwo = {n | n = 2^k}, additive complement (A complements B for large integers), and the specialized IsComplementToPowersOfTwo.

sections.title: Counting Functions and Density Bounds
sections.summary: Defines the counting function A(N) = |A ∩ [N]| and three density conditions: HasDensityNOverLogN (target), HasLorentzDensity (weaker), and HasAsymptoticOptimalDensity (exact asymptotic via Filter.Tendsto).

sections.title: The Main Problem Statement
sections.summary: Formalizes Erdős Problem #221: existence of a set that is both a complement to powers of 2 and has density O(N/log N).

sections.title: Lorentz's Result (1954)
sections.summary: Axiomatizes Lorentz's first positive result with the weaker density O(N log log N / log N), leaving a log log N gap from the optimum.

sections.title: Ruzsa's Construction (1972)
sections.summary: Defines Ruzsa's constant C = 1/(5 log 2), the core set {5^n · m : 5^n ≥ C log m}, RuzsaSet = core + {0,1}, axiomatizes the primitive root property, and derives ruzsa_1972 solving the conjecture.

sections.title: Problem #221 SOLVED
sections.summary: States erdos_221_answer: the conjecture holds, witnessed by Ruzsa's set.

sections.title: Ruzsa's Exact Complement (2001)
sections.summary: Axiomatizes Ruzsa's 2001 refinement: an exact additive complement with asymptotically optimal density A(N) ~ N/log₂ N.

sections.title: Why N/log N is Tight
sections.summary: Proves optimal_density: the upper bound (Ruzsa) and lower bound (any complement needs Ω(N/log N)) match, completely determining the growth rate.

sections.title: Connection to Primitive Roots
sections.summary: Details the algebraic engine: ord_{5^n}(2) = φ(5^n) = 4·5^{n-1}, and the consequence that powers of 2 cover all coprime residues mod 5^n.

sections.title: Generalization to Arbitrary Bases
sections.summary: Defines GeneralizedComplement for arbitrary base g ≥ 2 and axiomatizes that sparse complements to {g^k} exist with density O(N/log N) for any base.

sections.title: Related Problems: Sumsets and Additive Bases
sections.summary: Connects to sumset covering (A + {2^k} covers large integers) and additive basis theory (A ∪ PowersOfTwo forms a thin basis of order 2).

sections.title: Summary Theorems
sections.summary: Three final theorems: erdos_221_summary (full package), erdos_221_main (elementary restatement), and erdos_221 (positive answer + optimality of N/log N).

conclusion.summary: Erdős Problem #221 is SOLVED with tight bounds. Ruzsa (1972) constructed a set $A = \{5^n m : 5^n \ge C \log m\} + \{0,1\}$ with density $O(N/\log N)$ that complements the powers of 2, resolving the problem affirmatively. The key algebraic ingredient is that 2 is a primitive root mod $5^n$ for all $n \ge 1$. A matching lower bound shows $N/\log N$ is the correct order, and Ruzsa's 2001 refinement achieves the exact asymptotic $N/\log_2 N$.
conclusion.implications: This result reveals a deep and unexpected connection between additive combinatorics and algebraic number theory: the additive covering problem for powers of 2 is solved using a multiplicative property (primitive roots mod powers of 5). The tight $N/\log N$ bound has implications for the general theory of additive complements to lacunary sequences, and the technique generalizes to powers of any base $g \ge 2$.
openQuestions: What is the exact leading constant in the asymptotic $A(N) \sim c \cdot N/\log_2 N$ for Ruzsa's optimal complement? The construction gives an upper bound but the sharp constant is unknown.
For which primes $p$ does the lifting property hold, i.e., 2 is a primitive root mod $p^n$ for all $n$? This is related to but distinct from Artin's conjecture on primitive roots.
Can the additive complement problem be studied for other lacunary sequences beyond geometric progressions, such as $\{n^2\}$ or $\{p_n\}$ (primes)?
Is there a structural characterization of all optimal complements to $\{2^k\}$, or is Ruzsa's construction essentially unique?
